TL;DR: Mortgage rates eased today, but borrowing costs are still expensive for many home buyers.

Mortgage rates dropped today, but anything above 7% still puts pressure on home buyers’ budgets.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage dropped to 7.24% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is 14 basis points lower than yesterday and three basis points lower than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.)

A significant drop is eye-catching, but you should consider mortgage interest rates' overall direction, not just what's going on today. While the economy never sleeps, markets are closed on the weekends. The rates you see Friday are unlikely to change much (if at all) until Monday.

Here are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for context:

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

Next week, the Nerds are waiting for the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index, due out Wednesday. It's the Federal Reserve's preferred measure of inflation, so investors will be watching closely. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates, but lenders anticipate its decisions, so mortgage rates often move before the Fed acts. Stubbornly high inflation is a big reason why we’re seeing upward pressure on mortgage rates right now.

If PCE shows inflation comes in hotter than expected, mortgage rates could climb as markets anticipate further Fed rate hikes. (An increase to the federal funds rate is already widely expected at the Fed’s Dec. 8-9 meeting.) A cooler reading could ease some pressure on mortgage rates for now.

I’m not getting my hopes up too high for meaningfully lower inflation, though. Last week's Producer Price Index showed wholesale inflation climbed 6.5% over the past year — its fastest pace in four years. Wholesale inflation measures the price businesses pay for things. When businesses’ costs go up, they could pass those along to consumers in the form of higher prices — keeping the flames of inflation alive.

Whether Wednesday's PCE brings relief or another helping of bad inflation news, we'll know before the turkey hits the table on Thursday.

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

» Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

#3096. Quantum-Proof Accounts Are Coming to the XRP Blockchain by 2028. That's Not Likely to Be a Game Changer for XRP.

With quantum computing risks looming on the horizon, the XRP Ledger is planning to take action to keep funds safe.

By Alex Carchidi – Nov 21, 2026 at 7:05AM EST

According to Ripple, the creator of XRP (XRP -1.65%), the XRP Ledger (XRPL) will have quantum-secure wallets by 2028. Ripple itself set that target date in April of this year, and the XRP Ledger Foundation officially placed the corresponding upgrade onto its roadmap on Nov. 4.

XRP could sure use a catalyst, with its price being down 73% from its all-time high set in July 2025. But making more secure wallets will probably not do what holders are hoping for regarding the coin's price, at least not outside a very narrow and improbable set of circumstances. Here's why this upgrade probably won't be a game changer.

First, let's get some clarity on what is even at stake with the issue of security against quantum computers.

In technical terms, each XRP wallet, like nearly all other crypto wallets, has a secret private key and also a public key that anyone can see on a wallet-scanning website. The private key is what grants access to move funds from the account.

Deriving the private key from the public one is impossible in practical terms with today's hardware. But a powerful enough quantum computer could theoretically do exactly that in the future, meaning an attacker with such a computer could steal funds from individual wallets and likely spark a mass exodus of capital once the theft was discovered.

In March of this year, Alphabet's Google researchers published a paper estimating that breaking the cryptography that secures most crypto wallets could be possible with a significantly weaker quantum computer than previously expected. In a survey published in March 2026, the Global Risk Institute found that experts put the odds of such a machine arriving within 10 years at 28% to 49%.

Therefore, the XRPL's target preparedness date of 2028 probably leaves it with a decent margin of error if quantum computers advance faster than anticipated due to quantum computing companies ramping up their efforts.

Plus, given that quantum computers are massive, complex systems, the first dangerous machines will probably belong to governments and the largest companies building them, not ordinary hackers. However, an owner of such a machine may not announce it.

The direct impact of XRPL wallets becoming quantum-secure on its price will almost certainly be minimal.

The upgrade will not increase demand for the coin on its own. And while financial institutions might find it appealing that the XRPL is quantum-secure in advance, it's unclear whether they're willing to pay anything for it.

However, adapting early could pay out big in one specific future scenario.

If a powerful enough quantum computer becomes widely available years before most cryptocurrencies have implemented security measures and it's successfully used to carry out a major crypto hack, capital might flee to XRP as a safe haven.

But don't hold your breath for that to happen; even if the XRPL is an early mover in this domain, there are many other quantum-secure blockchains already in existence, and likely more to come.

#3093. College Scholarship Breakdown: Types, Sponsors and Eligibility at a Glance

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Scholarships vary in what they pay for and who can apply. Understanding the differences can save you time during your application process.

Scholarships have become a standard part of applying for college. You can learn about scholarships in a variety of ways, but looking through an online database of available scholarships — the most common way — can be overwhelming.

Before you go searching for a scholarship, it's important to understand the types of scholarships available and how to identify the ones that give you the best chance of winning, which can save you time and potentially earn you more funding. Here’s what you need to know about scholarships to decide which ones are best for you.

Scholarships are often funded by three groups: private organizations, institutions like universities, and government agencies. None is better than the other when it comes to awarding funds.

Nonprofit organizations and clubs that are looking for students either majoring in or researching certain fields, or who have experience volunteering in a specific field.

Companies that want to support all students or only fund those majoring in a field that relates to the companies’ industries.

Financial institutions, such as banks or credit unions, that want to support their community or their members.

Individuals or families that are funding private scholarships, usually in memory of a loved one.

Universities and colleges that are offering funds to students who attend their campuses.

Research organizations that want to fund students who will research in their areas of interest and further their causes.

These scholarships generally are provided by local, state or federal government agencies for a variety of reasons. Despite being funded by a government agency, the scholarships do not require you to pay back the money — unlike federal student loans.

Some scholarships pay for anything related to college expenses, including tuition, room and board, books and supplies, and more. Other scholarships limit what you can pay for with the funds, such as only tuition or tuition along with books. It’s important to look at this restriction when applying for scholarships to ensure the funds will go toward what you need to cover.

Merit scholarships require you to show excellence or achievements in your schoolwork, through talents and abilities, and even leadership or service work. Because these types of awards can be highly competitive, merit scholarships might require more than just achievements, such as volunteer or leadership experience. This means merit-based scholarships can overlap with other types of scholarship categories. Here are some examples of merit-based scholarships:

Merit scholarships often require you to have earned a minimum grade point average (GPA). The minimum GPA depends on the scholarship but often ranges from 2.0 to 4.0, with more competitive scholarships usually requiring higher GPAs. Scholarships with lower GPA minimums are more likely to consider additional factors, such as financial need.

Some merit scholarships might require a minimum ACT or SAT score instead of a GPA — or in addition to a minimum GPA.

Merit scholarships might also require applicants to have participated in activities outside of their schoolwork. This is common for scholarships that require membership in a certain group or organization. For example, membership in agricultural clubs, such as 4-H or FFA, and scouting groups, such as the National Eagle Scout Association, appear in scholarship requirements.

Some scholarships emphasize volunteering or community service and only consider applicants who have that experience. Applications vary in how detailed their requirements can be. Some scholarships want only a general description of where and how you’ve volunteered, and others might require experience with a service project that shows more leadership experience or time volunteering with a certain type of organization.

Scholarships that are awarded to students who can’t afford college are called need-based scholarships.

Unmet financial need is the difference between what it will cost you to attend college and what you can afford to pay. Because calculating how much you can afford is a complicated process, many scholarships refer to your FAFSA to document your financial need.

Some scholarship requirements may be as straightforward as demonstrating that you have financial need, but some scholarships might have income limits. However, income restrictions are less common.

Athletic scholarships are for — you guessed it — athletes. They are usually offered by colleges and universities to recruit athletes onto their collegiate teams and can be competitive. Which sports have scholarships available and the scholarship amounts vary by college.

Even though the main criterion for an athletic scholarship is being good at your sport, you’ll likely still need to show that you can keep up with your schoolwork. Most athletic scholarships require students to earn a minimum GPA or test scores to remain eligible while they’re in college.

Some scholarships are designated for students majoring in a general field, such as science or education, but others can be for very specific areas of study. For example, a scholarship for students majoring in a natural resource field could include majors in biology, ecology, wildlife biology, conservation education, forestry, soils and hydrology. However, a stricter scholarship might state that students have to major in more specific topics, such as biochemistry or microbial ecology.

Scholarships are available for active and former members of the military and members of their families. In addition to federal funds available for veterans to attend college, private organizations and some universities have scholarships for veterans to offset the cost of a degree.

Which family members can apply for funds depends on the individual scholarship. For example, some scholarships extend to children or spouses of veterans, but some go as far in a family tree as great-grandchildren.

Veteran- and military-focused scholarships might require that applicants or their family members enlisted in a certain branch, served during a particular time or conflict, or meet a certain rank or status such as receiving disability. Scholarships might also require that the applicant be a wartime veteran or family member of a wartime veteran; not all veterans meet this status.

Scholarships are also awarded to people who identify with a certain group. Common examples of identity-based scholarships include those for people who have disabilities, belong to certain ethnic or religious groups, identify as LGBTQIA+ or are first-generation students. Some identity-based scholarships require applicants to meet several criteria, such as belonging to more than one identity group.

Outside of what would be considered standard DEI groups, there are scholarships for applicants who identify with less common groups, such as veganism, homelessness and model railroad builders.

The best scholarships for you depend on your situation. For example, if you are a skilled athlete with a good academic record, going for an athletic scholarship might give you the most funding. On the other hand, if you’re going to research a topic that isn’t common, looking for scholarships that support your research topic might be your best bet because competition could be lower.

Good tactics to figure out which scholarships are worth your time include:

Think of the skills, talents, experience and identities that are unique to you. For example, being a child of a veteran immediately qualifies you for scholarships with fewer applicants than scholarships open to everyone. Likewise, if you embrace a certain ethnicity, identify with a specific group or have experience with a type of work, you might qualify for scholarships that appreciate and recognize those attributes more than the average scholarship.

Apply if you think you're eligible. Don’t apply to just a few scholarships and hope you get them. Instead, apply for as many scholarships as you can and for which you’re eligible. This increases your chances of receiving funds. Even small scholarships can make a big impact when you add several of them together.

Understand how you can use the money. If you already have a scholarship that covers only books, applying for the same type of scholarship isn’t helpful if you don’t need the extra funds. Instead, look for scholarships that cover the costs you have remaining.

Not sure where to look? Our sister site Scholarships360.org provides students with vetted scholarship opportunities. That would be a good place to start.

#3091. Greg Abel Just Approved a Record $9.6 Billion in Stock Buybacks for Berkshire Hathaway Last Quarter, More Than Double the Pace Set in the Second Quarter. Is Berkshire Still a Buy as Shares Sit Near All-Time Highs?

Berkshire Hathaway is using its cash hoard to buy its own stock, which suggests the board believes it's still a good investment.

By Reuben Gregg Brewer – Nov 21, 2026 at 7:15AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Berkshire Hathaway ›

Greg Abel took over as CEO of Berkshire Hathaway (BRKA -0.47%)(BRKB -0.36%) at the start of 2026, when longtime CEO Warren Buffett stepped down. It was the biggest change at the company in decades. However, Buffett hand-picked Abel and helped to train him for the top spot. And yet, Abel has been surprisingly aggressive in his decision to repurchase Berkshire Hathaway's own stock, something Buffett was very careful about.

With Berkshire Hathaway's stock sitting near all-time highs, is it worth buying? Abel clearly thinks the answer is yes. If you have been thinking about buying the stock, you may want to listen to what his actions are saying.

Before digging into Berkshire Hathaway's repurchase, it is worth taking a quick look at another investment Greg Abel orchestrated during the quarter. But that story actually goes back to the first big acquisition under Abel: Taylor Morrison Home. It was an $8.5 billion purchase, with Abel specifically stating, "Over time, we expect to unify our site-built homebuilding operations into a combined platform enabling us to deliver the dream of homeownership to more Americans."

Home builders are deeply out of favor today, with home affordability already an issue even before interest rates started to rise (making mortgages more expensive). It was an opportunistic acquisition that was reminiscent of Warren Buffett's investment approach. This is why it was notable that Abel nearly doubled the company's position in publicly traded homebuilder Lennar (LEN +1.01%) during the third quarter. Abel is essentially buying into an industry he believes is mispriced by the market, extending the bet he made with Taylor Morrison Home. Again, this is really no different than what Buffett had done many times before in his long tenure as CEO.

The key point here is that Abel hasn't suddenly and dramatically changed the way Berkshire Hathaway operates. Historically, the company bought back its own shares only when it believed the stock was trading below its intrinsic value. Of course, that value is determined by the company, and it doesn't disclose the figure it arrives at. But the fact that Greg Abel is buying back stock is a clear indication that he sees value, even though the share price is near all-time highs.

The pace of the share repurchase picked up materially between the second and third quarters, too. In the second quarter, the financial giant bought $4.5 billion worth. In the third quarter, that more than doubled to $9.6 billion. Those are huge numbers, but there's an important nuance here that shows up on the balance sheet.

Far too often, companies take on debt to fund stock buybacks. Berkshire Hathaway ended the third quarter with roughly $377 billion in cash. That is a massive sum of money, so the $9.6 billion won't weaken the company's financial position. In fact, the company has more cash now than it did at the start of 2026, when it had $373 billion. Buying back Berkshire Hathaway shares is just another investment decision, and it isn't hugely material to the company's operations or financial position.

Essentially, Greg Abel's actions suggest he and the board believe Berkshire Hathaway's stock is worth buying today. These weren't bold moves, but that's not the point. The buyback is a signal, and it's pretty clear: Berkshire Hathaway stock is attractive even at current levels.

Would it be fair to suggest that Berkshire Hathaway is a screaming buy? Probably not. However, if you have been thinking about buying the stock yourself, don't let the stock's lofty price tag scare you away. After all, that fact didn't scare Abel away.

#3088. Breakfast News: When Tech Wobbles, Dividends Pay

Motley Fool analysts share their favorite dividend stocks as tech stocks wobble.

By TMF Breakfast News – Nov 21, 2026 at 7:30AM EST

Tech stocks have had a bumpy few weeks, to say the least. Before we continue this edition of Breakfast News, here are some words of wisdom from Fools:

“When a sell-off is driven more by fear than by fundamentals, it often creates opportunities for patient investors. My advice is the same as it was in 2020. Keep your emergency fund intact, don’t sell in a panic, and if you have long-term money to invest, consider putting it to work in great businesses at better prices.”

“We are technically in correction territory today. My rule in moments like this is simple: if you worry about short-term volatility, avoid unprofitable companies or cash-burning businesses trading on high price-to-sales (P/S) multiples. When liquidity tightens, the market stops being generous. Ideally, we plan to keep our investments for at least five years, and be diversified across asset classes, market caps, industries and geographies. Ultimately, the market will find its footing, and it is important we do not lose our heads in the meantime.”

The Nasdaq-100 has fallen more than 13% in one month, as of this writing. Dividend payers, meanwhile, have held up well, and many have risen.

In October, the market’s dividend yield was about 1.1%, the lowest in 155 years. But dividends have driven a big share of the market’s long-term returns. In their recent FoolFest session, Investing for Income: Dividends and More, TMF analysts Anthony Schiavone and Jason Moser showed how big: If you’d invested $100 in 1871, price gains alone would have turned it into about $168,000. With dividends reinvested, you’d have almost $114 million.

We asked four of our analysts their favorite dividend stocks right now. Here’s what they said.

The cornerstone of Berkshire Hathaway’s (BRKB -0.36%) sustained success, as articulated by Warren Buffett in his 2022 shareholder letter, is the identification of companies that consistently increase their dividends at an above-average pace over extended periods.

As Buffett explained, dividend “growth occurred every year, just as certain as birthdays,” highlighting Coca-Cola (KO +0.94%) and American Express (AXP -3.02%) as prime examples. Buffett labeled dividend growth as the “secret sauce” to Berkshire’s investment philosophy.

I think Domino’s Pizza (DPZ -1.04%), which Berkshire bought in 2024 and sold in early 2026, also has the attributes of a dividend darling. The company has an enduring, asset-light business model that generates a ton of free cash flow, which is used to shrink the share count and to pay consistently higher dividends. That’s the secret sauce for me: higher dividends with a shrinking share count.

GE Aerospace (GE -2.90%) won’t land on many dividend enthusiast lists, because it only emerged as a stand-alone aviation business in April 2024. But in the 2.5 years since, GE has raised its quarterly dividend by 68% cumulatively, and given its lean business model and market position, I believe we’ll see additional aggressive hikes ahead.

GE merges AI capability with kaizen (continuous improvement) processes through its “Flight Deck” platform to speed production processes and reduce costs. It’s on track to end 2026 with stellar net income and free cash flow margins — both around 18%. And demand stretches to the horizon given the aerospace industry’s supply-constrained state.

GE’s commercial services backlog of $170 billion alone is more than triple total company annual revenue of approximately $51 billion. For investors seeking diversification from technology investments, note that backlog orders tied to jet engines are likely firmer than those linked to AI infrastructure (and I invest in both types of backlogs!).

The current dividend yield is 0.6%, but there’s room for growth through dividend payout increases, given GE’s healthy payout ratio of only 20%. This capable aerospace giant stands out for its excellent financial condition and relative safety for dividend investors.

Five-year price prediction: $562.78, implying an annualized return of around 11%.

Cisco Systems (CSCO -4.29%) rarely steals the spotlight from flashier chipmakers, yet this networking giant has quietly become a reliable dividend compounder.

Cisco has raised its quarterly payout every year for 15 consecutive years, currently paying $1.68 per share annually, for a roughly 1.7% yield. With a conservative earnings payout ratio under 45% and generous free cash flow growth, there is plenty of runway for future dividend increases.

Under the hood, Cisco’s business is far stronger and more tied to artificial intelligence than many income investors realize. In its fiscal Q1 2027 report, Cisco posted its fastest revenue and earnings growth in over 15 years, with quarterly sales jumping 24% to a record $18.5 billion.

Management also doubled its full-year forecast for hyperscaler AI infrastructure revenue to $9 billion as cloud giants snap up its high-speed switches and optical gear to connect massive AI clusters, all while returning $3.7 billion to shareholders through dividends and buybacks.

Trading around 18 times forward earnings with an entrenched enterprise and AI footprint, Cisco gives long-term investors a dependable income stream backed by accelerating growth.

Pharma boasts a range of dividend payers with long, reliable histories. But it’s hard to beat AbbVie (ABBV +0.94%) right now. The company’s 50+ year history of increasing its annual dividend goes back way before its 2013 spin-out from Abbott.

Its yield, around 2.5%, is attractive and sustainable, with a reasonable payout ratio (based on cash flow) — a true Dividend Aristocrat. And the company has already navigated past its most difficult patent expiration, making growth easier going forward.

Pfizer (PFE -0.51%), on the other hand, offers a very different profile. Earlier this year, I said that they were paying out all their cash flow (and then some) to cover their dividend. The yield has come down a bit (to around 6%) thanks to price appreciation, and their payout ratio, while still stretched, is a little less alarming at about 83%.

Nevertheless, recent revenue growth is likely to be short-lived — a new round of patent expirations peaks in 2027-2028. Pfizer recently committed to maintaining its dividend, but my guess is that they’ll cut it in the next few years, so higher yields aren’t always better!

Dividends rarely make headlines, but they pay you in cash regardless of what the market does. That steady income makes it easier to stay invested when prices fall. And when a company keeps raising its dividend, it’s also signaling confidence that it will keep earning the money to pay it.

Still, not all dividends are equal. A very high yield could be a trap if the stock price has fallen because the business is struggling and the payout is unsustainable. So look past the yield. Check whether the company earns enough cash to cover its dividend and whether its debt is under control. The best dividend stocks keep paying you more over time.

If you could own only one dividend stock, which would it be and why?

Discuss with friends and family, or become a member to hear what your fellow Fools are saying!

#3083. Is This 6%-Yielding Dividend Stock a Bargain or a Trap? Its Payout Eats Up About 90% of Cash Flow.

Here's the case for and against buying the high-yielding logistics stock.

By Matt DiLallo – Nov 21, 2026 at 7:30AM EST

10 stocks we like better than United Parcel Service ›

UPS (UPS -2.65%) stands out for its dividend yield these days. At 6%, it's several times higher than the S&P 500's 1.1% yield. That wide divergence might have you wondering whether it's a trap or a bargain.

Here's a look at the case for and against investing in UPS stock right now.

UPS recently reported its third-quarter earnings, giving investors a glimpse into the safety of its dividend, which the company has maintained or increased every year since its 1999 IPO. The metric that matters most for dividend investors is its cash flow. UPS has generated $6 billion in cash from operations through the first nine months of this year. Meanwhile, its free cash flow, after accounting for payments made under its Driver Choice Program, was $4.2 billion. That was just barely enough to cover its dividend, which cost the company $4.1 billion.

UPS now expects to generate about $6.1 billion in free cash flow for the full year and anticipates paying $5.4 billion in dividends, subject to board approval. That would put its payout ratio at roughly 89%, which is high. If market conditions unexpectedly deteriorate, its dividend could be at risk of a reduction. On a positive note, the company has $6.8 billion in cash on its balance sheet, providing a bit more cushion.

UPS is in the middle of a strategic transition away from less profitable Amazon volumes toward higher-margin business, including healthcare logistics. The company is nearing the completion of its Amazon glide-down and the reconfiguration of its cost structure to align with these lower volumes. Its third-quarter report showed that this strategy is delivering results. Its revenue rose 6.7%, with growth across all segments. That gave the company the confidence to boost its full-year outlook, including for free cash flow.

The company is now on track to deliver $7.28 per share of adjusted earnings. At its recent $110 share price, UPS trades at about 15x earnings. That's a bargain compared to the broader market (the S&P 500 trades at over 23x earnings).

UPS wouldn't have to grow very fast to deliver strong total returns from here. With a 6% yield, the company could deliver double-digit total returns with around 4% annual earnings-per-share growth (assuming it maintained its current low valuation multiple). Meanwhile, if earnings grow faster and its valuation improves, UPS could deliver much stronger total returns, potentially in the mid-teens.

I lean toward bargain, but this isn't a dividend stock you can bank on just yet. I'm watching three things. First, revenue needs to continue rising. Second, I want to see next year's free cash flow guidance, since it needs to remain well above $5.4 billion to cover the dividend. Finally, I want to make sure debt doesn't creep up to fund the payout. If UPS continues executing its turnaround strategy and gets back on a sustainable growth trajectory, it's a bargain at the current price. However, if it faces a setback, the dividend could be at risk.

Palo Alto Networks (PANW) is a provider of cybersecurity solutions across network, cloud, security operations, AI and identity. Following a discussion with management, BTIG analyst Gray Powell reiterated a buy rating on PANW and raised his price target to $425 from $404.

After a review of Palo Alto's product-level growth catalysts, Powell sees clear upside to both revenue and next-generation security (NGS) annual recurring revenue (ARR) in fiscal 2027. He expects PANW to deliver pro forma revenue growth of more than 17%, above the consensus estimate of 14.6%, and NGS ARR growth of more than 26% versus the Street's expectation of 24.5%.

Over the past five years, the Palo Alto business mix, has moved to higher-growth product areas and new markets. from what was earlier viewed as a hardware-centric network security company, Powell said. The 5-star analyst estimates that hardware firewalls and attached subscriptions now account for less than 50% of revenue.

Meanwhile, high-growth solutions, including Prisma SASE, software firewalls, Cortex XSIAM, Chronosphere and Idira now represent more than 35% of PANW's revenue. "Investors may not fully realize the growth potential within PANW's platform story," Powell said.

BTIG is optimistic about the prospects of Chronosphere in observability, CyberArk in identity and software firewalls and Prisma AIRS in the network and AI security business.

Powell ranks No. 320 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 61% of the time, delivering an average return of 17.3%. See Palo Alto Networks KPIs on TipRanks.

In a research note on September 30, Rosenblatt analyst Scott Devitt reiterated a buy rating on e-commerce and cloud computing platform Amazon (AMZN), raising his price target to $360 from $335. Fears that agentic commerce poses a major threat to Amazon's advertising business seem "overstated," he said.

Devitt noted that the growing adoption of personal agents and AI shopping assistants has sparked concern about displacement of Amazon's retail media business. But the 5-star analyst remains bullish, given Amazon's ability to adapt to changing consumer behavior, as it's done in the past.

Additionally, Devitt argues that even if an AI agent helps a shopper discover a product, Amazon can still handle the purchase and delivery, keeping much of the transaction value. He highlighted that management believes that existing Amazon shoppers will likely continue to start their shopping journey on the platform because it has better personalization, accurate pricing and inventory information that third-party agents still lack.

Overall, Devitt expects Amazon's retail business to prove a net beneficiary of agentic commerce. Fewer clicks would not hurt the company if the value of each remaining click and overall volumes keep rising, he said. The argument is that even if Amazon loses some sponsored ad revenue over the next few years, it would likely be only a small part of the company's total business and could be offset by growth in other areas.

"Consistent with our AI framework, we continue to view Amazon as one of the most resilient leaders in our coverage, combining owned compute infrastructure with a physical fulfillment moat," said Devitt. His bullish view is supported, Devitt said, by expectations that Amazon Web Services (AWS) will exit the year at a more than 45% growth rate with continued margin improvement.

#3079. Is AMD the Stock to Buy With Nvidia in Limbo?

AMD may be the popular pick, but is it the right one?

By Keithen Drury – Nov 21, 2026 at 7:40AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Advanced Micro Devices ›

With all the unknowns surrounding Nvidia (NVDA -14.01%) right now, some investors are starting to wonder if Advanced Micro Devices (AMD -13.25%) is the semiconductor stock to turn to instead. This is a natural progression because the two are competitors in the data center space.

Any analysis of a possible change should start by asking whether AMD is a viable alternative. Does AMD have problems of its own to contend with?

My analysis suggests there's at least one issue that investors must watch out for, and I think it is definitive in determining which stock is the better pick right now. Let me explain.

AMD is commonly viewed as an alternative to Nvidia. Nvidia's data center products were more advanced than AMD's when the initial artificial intelligence build-out kicked off, and that allowed Nvidia to seize early market share. First-mover advantage can be difficult to overcome, and with a significant majority of data center computing infrastructure being built for Nvidia products, AMD has found itself in a deep hole.

However, the biggest problem AMD faces isn't hardware; it's software. Nvidia's CUDA software is considered better than AMD's ROCm software, although AMD has improved recently. Still, this is an advantage Nvidia holds over AMD, and it has created a gap unlikely to be closed.

AMD has seen increased success in the data center realm as clients look for cheaper alternatives to Nvidia GPUs, which can be quite expensive due to high demand. During the third quarter, AMD's data center revenue rose 97% year over year to $8.5 billion. However, because AMD also has significant consumer and embedded processor divisions, the results are a bit worse when the entire company is examined. Companywide, AMD's revenue rose 45% year over year to $13.4 billion. Considering that Nvidia is posting $100 billion-plus in quarterly revenue, AMD is a much smaller company.

Normally, being a smaller company is an advantage because it's easier to grow faster. But that hasn't been the case here. Nvidia has outpaced AMD's growth every step of the way, which is impressive considering the fact that it's almost 9 times larger than AMD. I think this speaks to the unbreakable lead that Nvidia has built from a technological and market-share standpoint.

However, with new leadership coming to power at Nvidia, it could shift how the company approaches product development and the market. This could lead to a shifting landscape over the next five years, but as of now, Nvidia remains the leader, with AMD in second place.

That's still not the reason I'm avoiding investing in AMD. AMD has stock problems of its own.

AMD is one of the more expensive stocks in the market right now. If you use next year's earnings projections to value the stock, it trades for about 29 times next year's earnings.

AMD PE Ratio (Forward 1y) data by YCharts

That's a pretty expensive price tag. Not even some of the AI hyperscalers have that expensive a price tag. Furthermore, Nvidia is far cheaper, trading at around 10 times next year's earnings.

While I understand that Nvidia deserves something of a price discount due to leadership uncertainty and the sources of its sales, 10 times next year's earnings is an absolute steal. Nvidia could lose half of its earnings and still trade at less than 20 times next year's earnings.

That's a huge pricing mismatch, and I think that the market has gone too far in discounting Nvidia. As a result, I don't think that AMD is the best stock to buy during Nvidia's turmoil. Instead, Nvidia is likely the best stock to buy, as the market has far overblown what is going on with the stock.

#3075. Here's How Many Shares of Starbucks You’d Need to Cover $744 in Coffee Using Dividends Alone

Making a five-figure investment for free coffee may prove to be a tall order, especially after this stock's recent rally.

By Thomas Niel – Nov 21, 2026 at 7:40AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Starbucks ›

"Stop buying coffee out" has become commonplace personal finance advice, but is there a way to invest and cover your monthly Starbucks (SBUX -1.28%) bill? Let's say you go to Starbucks a few times a week, which, over the course of a year, can really add up: 150 trips a year at $4.96 per cup, or just under $5, comes out to $744 annually.

That said, for a five-figure investment, you could pay for these coffees from your dividends alone. However, in terms of potential gains from holding the stock, is it worth it? Not necessarily.

Following Starbucks' latest dividend increase, shares in what is one of the largest consumer discretionary companies now pay $0.63 per share quarterly. That comes to $2.52 per share in annual dividend payments. Divide $744 by $2.52 per share, and you get 296 Starbucks shares needed to cover this expense. Starbucks stock currently trades for around $106.50 per share, meaning you would need around $31,524 to enter this position.

Any way you slice it, that's a tall order. Even as annual dividend growth has averaged nearly 8% over the past five years, the latest dividend increase was only 1.6%. If low dividend growth persists, the price of a cup of Starbucks coffee could outpace the payouts. Also, don't assume buying today means trading lower dividend growth for the potential for greater gains down the road.

The company's "Back to Starbucks" turnaround, focused on improving the in-store experience, has been in motion for over two years now. Recent results, including a 7.2% increase in same-store sales during the September-ended quarter, have investors very confident about further improvements in growth and profitability.

However, after this rally, the stock trades at 33.5 times forward earnings, a big premium to peers like McDonald's. Although further strong quarterly results could help sustain this valuation, any sort of earnings hiccup could quickly send shares back in the wrong direction. Considering this, I would skip buying Starbucks shares for now.

#3068. Warren Buffett Successor Greg Abel Piled $28 Billion Into This Stock in the First Half of 2026, But Opted Not to Buy More at a Lower Price Last Quarter

Has something changed with Abel's biggest investment so far?

By Adam Levy – Nov 21, 2026 at 7:58AM EST

Greg Abel has already started to make his mark on Berkshire Hathaway (BRKA -0.47%) (BRKB -0.36%). The CEO took over the job from Warren Buffett at the start of the year, and he's since gone to work deploying tens of billions of dollars worth of capital for shareholders. He completed the acquisitions of OxyChem and Taylor Morrison Homes for a total of $18 billion. He reinitiated repurchases of the stock, buying back more than $16 billion worth of Berkshire through October. And he's added considerably to Berkshire marketable equity portfolio, including buying an estimated $28 billion worth of Alphabet (GOOG -2.59%) (GOOGL -2.70%) stock.

While Abel increased his share repurchases in the third quarter and continued to look for opportunities to fully acquire other companies, he stopped buying Alphabet shares. That's despite the fact that the share price moved meaningfully lower than the price he paid in Alphabet's $10 billion private placement with his company. Investors may be wondering if anything's changed for Alphabet since that purchase and whether it's worth buying right now.

Greg Abel. Image source: The Motley Fool.

Buffett built Berkshire Hathaway on the ethos of long-term buy-and-hold investing, and Abel has promised to maintain that philosophy in every investment decision he makes for the company. That said, a long-term outlook doesn't mean Buffett hasn't been known to quickly change his mind on a company, especially if things change. Only a handful of marketable equity investments have stuck around for Buffett's preferred holding period of "forever."

Buffett laid out the investment thesis for Alphabet, a position he initiated for Berkshire last year, in an interview this summer. It boils down to the fact that Alphabet has an opportunity to deploy a lot of capital and earn a high return on its invested capital doing so. In other words, Buffett believes Alphabet's massive AI build-out will produce exceptional cash flows over the long run.

While there are growing concerns that Alphabet won't achieve high returns on capital, the financial results so far suggest it's seeing excellent results. Alphabet's Google Cloud segment grew revenue 103% year over year last quarter while expanding its operating margin. That acceleration is tied to a ramp-up in investments starting in 2023, right in line with the timeline of how long it takes before breaking ground on new data center construction translates into placing servers and networking equipment available for rent on its platform.

Alphabet's reported payback period is well above that reported by other hyperscalers. Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian said it takes about two years for it to generate revenue equal to the cost of the average server for its cloud platform. However, its custom TPU systems have a payback period of half of that. Over time, a greater portion of Alphabet's capital expenditures will go toward revenue-generating servers and a greater share of those servers will be its own custom hardware with faster payback periods.

As such, it makes sense for Alphabet to raise capital and burn cash to build new data centers. The return on invested capital is extremely high and the opportunity is absolutely massive. It's playing out exactly as Buffett expects.

If Abel liked Alphabet stock at a price of $355 per share, which is what Berkshire paid for the stock in its private placement, he should like it even more at $280 per share, where it trades today.

The stock traded around $340 per share throughout the second half of the third quarter, so there was an opportunity for Abel to add to the position before the quarter ended at a price he was previously comfortable paying. However, Alphabet was already Berkshire's third-largest position as of the end of the third quarter, without any additional shares. That could push the bar higher for Abel to add to the position and increase Berkshire's portfolio concentration. (It's notably why I personally haven't added to my own position in Alphabet amid the pullback, as it already accounts for a significant portion of my portfolio.)

For investors without a significant position in Alphabet, though, right now looks like an incredible buying opportunity for the stock. Shares trade at just 21 times forward earnings expectations, and the long-term growth potential of its cloud computing segment (which includes its TPU system sales) looks better than ever.

Considering the drop in share price pushed Alphabet to become a much smaller portion of Berkshire's portfolio, Abel may be inclined to buy more shares again this quarter after last quarter's pause.

#3062. Got $500? 2 Quantum Computing Stocks to Buy Right Now

Two quantum companies, one built on atoms and one built on light, for a modest $500 bet.

By Micah Zimmerman – Nov 21, 2026 at 8:00AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Infleqtion ›

Five hundred dollars doesn't stretch very far anymore. It buys a nice pair of headphones, a few weeks of groceries, or one good weekend away. It can also get you a small stake in one of the strangest machines anybody is trying to build.

The idea behind quantum computing is easier to picture than it sounds. A regular computer bit works like a light switch: on or off. A qubit is closer to a dimmer that can sit anywhere in between, and when qubits are linked, they can work together to explore a huge number of possibilities. The problem is that qubits are as fragile as a soufflé. A tiny bit of heat or vibration and the whole thing collapses.

The fix is the "logical qubit," a team of physical qubits that works like a choir. If one singer drifts off key, the others hold the note. Whoever builds lots of reliable logical qubits first wins the race.

Here are two quantum computing companies working on this very issue that I'd be willing to split a $500 investment in.

Infleqtion (INFQ -13.43%) traps single atoms with lasers and uses them as qubits. In September 2026, it said it had linked 30 logical qubits in a single computation using just 80 physical qubits, hitting its 2026 goal. "Delivering 30 logical qubits is an important step on our technology roadmap," CEO Matt Kinsella said.

Its hardware is already in real machines. Infleqtion's processor powers Shunkai, Japan's first working full-stack neutral-atom quantum computer. "Bringing a full-stack quantum system into production operation is a meaningful step toward fault-tolerant quantum computing," said CTO Pranav Gokhale.

The part I like most is that the same atoms do other jobs today. Infleqtion's Tiqker clock keeps precise time when GPS is jammed, and it recently ran for two weeks straight aboard a U.S. Navy vessel. "The Navy needs dependable timing to navigate, communicate and coordinate operations in the field," Kinsella said. NASA also expanded its quantum gravity sensor contract, and the U.K. funded a compact radio-direction-finding system.

That government work is also its weak spot. Last quarter, it cost Infleqtion more to deliver its work than it earned, partly because of timing on the NASA gravity program and thin margins on a contract that was wrapping up. Spending is climbing fast too. Its operating loss was about five times larger than a year ago. The cash it raised through its special-purpose acquisition company (SPAC) merger gives it room for now.

Xanadu Quantum Technologies (XNDU -6.59%) uses particles of light as qubits. "Our chips compute without coolant," CEO Christian Weedbrook said, and they can be made with the same kind of silicon processes chipmakers already use.

Light's enemy is loss, meaning photons that leak away before the math is done. Weedbrook called it "our most important engineering challenge," but added, "This is primarily a challenge of engineering, not physics." In November, Xanadu and HyperLight cut the loss in a key optical switch by nearly two-thirds.

It's also lining up help. Xanadu signed hardware partnerships with GlobalFoundries (GFS -8.68%), ASML (ASML -6.63%), and Bluefors, and launched Backline, error-correction software built with Advanced Micro Devices Inc. (AMD -13.25%). Mitsubishi Chemical used its algorithms to model semiconductor materials, and Royal Bank of Canada and Booz Allen use its software to train staff. Canada is putting about $140 million toward Inception, a Toronto photonics plant Xanadu expects to start using early next year.

Here's the catch: Xanadu barely has revenue, and it's choosing to keep it that way for now. "Pursuing revenue before meaningful quantum utility or selling systems prematurely would ultimately divert talent and resources," Weedbrook said. Its target for a commercially viable machine is 2029 or 2030, and until then, its cash burn keeps rising. Xanadu can also sell more shares through an existing program, and an executive said the company weighs that "almost on a day-by-day basis."

Quantum stocks like these trade on hope as much as results, so I'd treat both like small-cap stocks and size them so a bust stings rather than hurts. I'd put about $300 into Infleqtion, since it's already getting paid for its atoms, and $200 into Xanadu as the long shot. One is earning while it builds. The other is betting everything on getting the light right, and $500 lets you own both stories without needing either one to be perfect.

#3057. AbbVie (ABBV) Stock Just Got a 5.2% Dividend Increase. Here's How Many Shares You Need to Generate $1,000 a Year.

This pharmaceutical giant has hiked its payout for 53 years in a row, so it's likely to keep doing so.

By Selena Maranjian – Nov 21, 2026 at 8:10AM EST

If you're in the market for a healthcare stock for your long-term portfolio, pharmaceutical giant AbbVie (ABBV +0.94%) offers several compelling reasons to invest in.

Here's a closer look at AbbVie and some of those reasons to consider it. First, though, let's talk dividends.

AbbVie stock recently sported a dividend yield of 2.4%. That's quite solid, but it might have been higher had the stock not popped by 28% year to date (as of Nov. 18). (A stock's dividend yield is its total annual dividend amount divided by the stock price, so when the stock price rises, the yield falls, and vice versa.)

Better still, it's a growing dividend. The current $1.82 quarterly payout is up 5.2% from the previous $1.73, and up from $1.41 in 2022 and $0.57 in 2016. And AbbVie has hiked its payout for 53 years in a row, making it a Dividend King.

Let's say you're looking for $1,000 in annual income from AbbVie. How many shares would you need to own? The math is straightforward: The total payout for the year is $1.82 times four, or $7.28 for the year. Divide $1,000 by $7.28, and you'll get the needed number of shares: 137.36.

At a recent stock price of $284 per share, 137 shares will cost you... roughly $39,000.

But would you want to invest in AbbVie? I'm a shareholder myself, but I'd hesitate to jump in right now because the recent valuation seems a bit high. The recent price-to-sales ratio of 7.7, for example, is well above the five-year average of 5.4, and the forward-looking price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 17.6 is also well above the five-year average of 13.9.

So maybe just add it to your watch list, hoping for a lower entry point. Or just start a small position in it now -- as long as you aim to hang on for many years. Its last earnings report was good, with revenue up 10% year over year and immunology drugs Skyrizi and Rinvoq performing particularly well.

#3054. Stock Market Sell-Off: History Says This Is the Smartest Move Investors Can Make Right Now

Keep calm and carry on, the famous World War II slogan from Great Britain, is perfect advice for a bear market.

By Reuben Gregg Brewer – Nov 21, 2026 at 8:15AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Bright Horizon Energy ›

The S&P 500 index (^GSPC -3.70%) is near all-time highs despite multiple geopolitical conflicts, inflation, rising interest rates, and the risk of the AI bubble bursting. Wall Street is justifiably worried that a bear market could soon arrive. The smartest move you can make right now is to prepare yourself emotionally for a market downturn. My preferred approach is to distract myself with dividends. Here's why.

History is clear: a bear market is on the way, though nobody knows exactly when it will arrive, and your emotions will be taxed. It could be a sizable downturn, too, given the similarities between the artificial intelligence (AI) bubble today and the dot-com bubble at the turn of the century. I remember the dot-com crash very well. It was brutal.

Then, just as the market was finally putting that deep and prolonged bear market in the rearview mirror, the Great Recession hit. That economic downturn and the associated bear market were just as brutal. There were legitimate concerns that the global financial system might collapse. And yet, history is very clear: the S&P 500 index, generally considered "the market", has recovered after each bear market and gone on to hit new highs. So the best course of action during a big downturn is to stay invested.

Staying invested, unfortunately, is easier said than done. It is hard to remain calm as you watch the value of your portfolio decline day after day. Bear markets like the dot-com bust and the Great Recession are relentless, and you will almost certainly feel panic building as the days drag on to weeks, months, and even years.

Having invested through some really bad bear markets, I know exactly how hard they can be on one's emotional well-being. The fear you feel can take physical form in sleepless nights, an unsettled stomach, and mental stress. My cure for the emotional hit of market volatility has long been to focus on the dividends my income-focused portfolio throws off each month.

That may sound a bit like King Midas counting his gold, but I know from experience that watching my dividends helps me ignore stock price volatility. And I focus on owning a diverse collection of well-run dividend stocks, including Dividend Kings like Procter & Gamble (PG +0.91%), Federal Realty (FRT -0.14%), and Black Hills (BKH +0.55%), all of which have increased their dividend annually for at least 50 consecutive years. For reference, that's a consumer staples company, a REIT, and a utility, with diversification being another of my investment focuses.

However, the key piece of this story isn't that I track my dividends during bear markets. It is that I track them all of the time. I have a spreadsheet that I update every month, in bull markets and bear markets. I'm not waiting for the next bear-market stress test to deal with the emotional toll of a downturn. I'm proactively preparing right now and have been for years. Simply put, I've developed a habit of focusing on dividends rather than stock prices.

I'm not suggesting that stock prices aren't relevant. They most certainly are important. But I also know there will be another bear market, and that sticking to my long-term investment approach through it to benefit from the next bull market is likely to lead to the best outcome. So I invest in a way that prepares me to buy and hold, no matter what the market is doing. For me, that means buying reliable dividend stocks and focusing on dividends more than stock prices. It's how I keep calm and carry on, to quote the famous British World War II slogan.

Only you can decide what will help you stay calm during a bear market. For me, it's focusing on the dividends I collect from reliable dividend stocks. But the smartest move right now is to figure out what you need to do before the next bear market comes along. Once it is here, your emotions will be elevated, and that means you will be more likely to make the kind of short-term decisions that could be bad for your long-term performance. Don't wait; prepare today for the bear market that history says is on the way.

#3050. Junk bonds are 'flashing yellow.' Watch these warning signs

Cracks are forming in the junk bond market as investors demand higher payouts for owning the market's riskiest debt. It isn't time to ditch high-yield bonds, but investors should pay attention to the warning signs.

High-yield bonds now yield 8.1%, up from 7.22% a month ago. The increase reflects a jump in yields across the curve as investors bake in more inflation from high energy prices and other pressures, including concern about the deficit — hitting nearly $2 trillion in the fiscal year that ended Sept. 30.

The high-yield market is also showing stress on the credit side with spreads recently widening to levels not seen since April, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. Credit spreads are the difference in yield between the bonds and Treasurys of similar maturities. Wider spreads mean investors are demanding higher yields for holding corporate debt, viewing it as riskier.

Spreads are at 315 basis points in the overall high-yield market, higher than a year ago but still below levels in March when they reached 346 bps. One basis point equals one one-hundredth of a percent, or 0.01%.

The high-yield market consists of bonds rated BB+ by S&P and Fitch and Ba1 and under by Moody's. The lowest-rated cohort, CCC and below, has seen the most movement with spreads climbing dramatically over the past year to roughly 1,250 bps.

Right now, the high-yield market is "flashing yellow" but is "far from red," said Michael Arone, chief investment strategist at State Street Investment Management.

It makes sense that investors are demanding more compensation for taking on additional credit risk as borrowing costs rise, he said.

Yields are elevated across the board with the 10-year Treasury reaching its highest level since 2002 earlier in the week.

"The bigger question is whether this is simply a repricing of interest rate risk, or the beginning of a more fundamental reassessment of credit quality," Arone said.

He's in a wait-and-see mode since earnings are still growing, interest-coverage ratios remain good, and while default rates have ticked up some, he believes it is not concerning.

That said, the starting point in spreads is likely weighing on investors' psyche, since they are still low by historical standards.

"There's a small margin of error here, which I also think raises the anxiety level," Arone explained. "The compensation that investors are receiving for taking on this credit risk isn't overwhelming relative to history, and therefore subtle changes in credit spreads can be concerning."

While there may be concerns about part of the lower-rated market, the overall high-yield market is in good fundamental shape.

In fact, credit quality is at a record high, with BB bonds making up over 60% of the market compared with 38% prior to the global financial crisis, said Kelley Gerrity, a fixed income strategist at Morgan Stanley Investment Management.

"We've had higher-quality companies coming in, and with higher rates now, you also have more discipline from companies that are more indebted ... just because of the higher cost of capital, so that actually is creating a bit of a healthier picture as well," she said.

The lowest tier of high yield has always been more speculative, since the bonds have a higher default risk. Therefore, it's no surprise that they are the ones seeing the most widening in spreads, said Collin Martin, head of fixed income research and strategy at the Schwab Center for Financial Research.

The overall move in high-yield spreads have been "orderly," he said. "Are there cracks forming? I think the cracks are logical cracks with the lowest-rated bonds and it's too early to say that it's spreading to the broad credit market."

In addition, fluctuations within the CCC-rated and lower spreads have been idiosyncratic, Gerrity added. Morgan Stanley recently broke down the spreads in the lowest cohort into two buckets: performing assets and non-performing assets, which are defined as spreads above 1,000 bps.

The non-performing spread to worst is 2,818 bps, while the performing bucket — the biggest piece of the CCC market — is 461 bps, she said.

"It is isolated," she said. "I'm not necessarily sure that that will go away anytime soon, but it doesn't tell the story of overall concern and flashing caution for credit markets right now."

For now, investors should remain selective within higher yield, Gerrity advised.

"We're looking for the best relative value opportunities, and we think that exists within that single-B cohort, and so we're leaning into that," she said.

Investors should be concerned if there is a steep widening in the broader high-yield market.

But there's scant evidence of stress in the BB cohort. Spreads in that group are at 194 bps, up from 179 bps a year ago — although the move hasn't been in a straight line.

"We're going to be focusing our attention on what are considered some stronger businesses," Martin said. "If we start to see the markets demand higher spreads there also, that's what we'll be looking at to see if risks are really rising."

It's also important to understand that the Federal Reserve is raising rates in a strong economic environment, said R.J. Gallo, chief investment officer of global fixed income at Federated Hermes. The central bank is concerned about an inflation problem amid high fossil fuel prices due to the Iran war, while growth has been stronger than expected, he noted.

"With growth being good as the reason that the Fed is hiking, then you wouldn't expect high yield to blow out because growth means revenues stay up, means cash flow and profitability stays up," he explained.

High yield becomes a disaster when the economy is heading into a sharp economic downturn, Gallo said.

"That's when spreads really widen out," he said. "But a recession is not the odds-on bet. Now, talk to me in six months if the Fed keeps hiking over and over, if oil prices stay high for longer, well, then maybe we will start to wonder."

#3048. Bitcoin Has Traded Below Its 200-Week Average Only 8.4% of the Time. History Says This Is When Patient Investors Get Paid.

Past trends show that bearish moments are usually the best times to buy this cryptocurrency.

By Neil Patel – Nov 21, 2026 at 8:19AM EST

In typical fashion, Bitcoin (BTC -2.58%) is taking investors on a bumpy ride. The world's first and most valuable digital asset has had short spurts of positive momentum this year. But in the past month, the price has tanked 28% (as of Nov. 21), with a five-day drop of 9%.

Bitcoin is currently trading nearly 14% below its 200-week moving average (WMA). According to River, a Bitcoin financial services firm, the leading cryptocurrency has only been in this territory 8.4% of the time in its entire life. It's a rare occurrence, indeed, and it shows that bearish sentiment is ruling the narrative right now.

History says the bulls should stay patient. This is when investors get paid.

The 200 WMA smooths out Bitcoin's wild price swings. It tracks the average closing price over roughly four years, which coincides with the investment community’s view of the digital asset's full market cycle. This is why many long-term investors treat it as a baseline.

As of Nov. 21, the 200 WMA sits at $68,130, and Bitcoin is trading about 14% beneath it. According to River, Bitcoin purchased during past periods when it traded below its 200 WMA returned an average of 120% over the following year. The subsequent three-year gain is 582%. At those averages, $10,000 would have grown to $22,000 after 12 months and $68,200 after 36 months.

It all sounds so easy, but investors shouldn't take those figures at face value. Because Bitcoin has rarely traded this low relative to its long-term average, the sample size is small. Many of those episodes came when Bitcoin was a niche experiment a decade or more ago. At a $1.2 trillion market cap, the cryptocurrency is unlikely to compound at the same pace as in its early years. Still, the direction of the pattern is hard to ignore.

The recent drop also needs context. Every past Bitcoin bear market included several rallies of 25% or more. This time is similar. That last surge occurred in the back half of August and September.

However, depth is the noticeable change. So far, this downturn has been much more muted than prior ones. Bitcoin is 53% below its peak now.

There are many takeaways. A smaller fall suggests a more mature asset with steadier holders. It could mean the bottom isn't in yet, and it might leave less upside going forward.

Every bear market brings its own reason to declare Bitcoin dead. The past down cycle in 2022 saw major exchange failures that harmed the industry's reputation. Before that, there were worries about government intervention.

Today's fear is more technical in nature. Critics argue that advances in artificial intelligence and quantum computing could break Bitcoin's cryptography. This would undermine the network's security. That's a real concern for any industry in 2026 and beyond.

There's no reason to panic yet. The real threat is likely many years away, and the Bitcoin community, fully aware of how technology is rapidly evolving, can adapt. Network updates can bolster the cryptographic setup over time.

There's also a track record worth noting. The Bitcoin network has operated for over 17 years with virtually no outages. That's a remarkable streak for any piece of financial infrastructure.

The smart money is paying attention. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filings show that many of Wall Street's biggest companies added to their Bitcoin positions last quarter. But the leading cryptocurrency probably still accounts for less than 0.1% in most of their clients’ portfolios, River says. That's a very tiny percentage among powerful companies with trillions of dollars in assets under management. A modest allocation bump could bring in demand and translate into substantial buying pressure.

Of course, Bitcoin is no sure thing. It's volatile, and past performance offers no guarantees.

That's where dollar-cost averaging comes in. Investors commit a fixed sum at regular intervals, whether the price is up or down. You avoid market timing, and in periods like the current one, a fixed sum gets you more Bitcoin.

Just remember to never invest more than you're willing to lose, and keep your eyes on the long term.

#3039. The 1 Thing I'll Be Watching When Broadcom Reports on Dec. 9

The chip designer has beaten its own AI forecast three quarters straight. Can the next outlook keep 2027 on track?

By Daniel Sparks – Nov 21, 2026 at 8:26AM EST

Broadcom (AVGO -12.19%) shares have dropped about $135 apiece since their record close on June 2, putting the stock roughly 28% under that peak at about $347 as of this writing. The chip designer reports results for the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026 (the period ended Nov. 1, 2026) after the market closes on Wednesday, Dec. 9.

There'll be lots of numbers in that release. But one line matters more to me than the rest: artificial intelligence (AI) semiconductor revenue. I'll be checking it twice -- once for the quarter Broadcom just wrapped up, against the $21.7 billion management forecast in September, and once for what the company expects in the first quarter of fiscal 2027.

After all, AI chips made up 56% of Broadcom's revenue in its latest quarter, and they accounted for over 80% of its year-over-year revenue growth.

Broadcom has made a habit of landing a bit above its own AI forecasts this year. In the first quarter of fiscal 2026 (the period ended Feb. 1, 2026), AI semiconductor revenue was $8.4 billion, against the $8.2 billion management had forecast. The fiscal second quarter brought $10.8 billion, against a $10.7 billion forecast. And the fiscal third quarter (the period ended Aug. 2) delivered $16.7 billion, over the $16.0 billion management had guided for.

Growth has accelerated the whole way, too. Year-over-year AI revenue growth rose from 106% in fiscal Q1 to 143% in fiscal Q2 and 221% in fiscal Q3. For fiscal Q4, management expects 236%.

In other words, Broadcom's guidance has leaned a little conservative. But the beats have been small -- between around 1% and 4% above the forecast. I'm not expecting a blowout in fiscal Q4, then. AI revenue at or a bit above $21.7 billion would show me the company is still on the schedule management laid out.

A result under $21.7 billion would break that streak for the first time this fiscal year.

Management's goal for next year is about $115 billion of AI revenue in fiscal 2027 -- almost double the $58 billion or so it expects for fiscal 2026. And on its September earnings call, Broadcom said it doesn't plan to update that figure every quarter. That arguably makes each quarterly forecast the best checkpoint investors have.

Do the math, and $115 billion comes to almost $29 billion a quarter on average. That's about a third higher than the fiscal fourth-quarter forecast. If AI revenue rose at an even pace from $21.7 billion, the first quarter of fiscal 2027 would likely need to land somewhere near $24 billion to keep the year on track.

A first-quarter forecast in the mid-$20 billion range, then, should be a sign the doubling is on schedule. A forecast closer to $22 billion might mean more of next year's growth is being shifted into the second half of fiscal 2027.

Management sounded confident in September.

"Our demand actually exceeds this outlook, and we will work to improve supply," said CEO Hock Tan.

If that holds, the first-quarter forecast might land above my rough math. Either way, Dec. 9 is the first chance to check.

After a 28% fall, I don't think Broadcom needs a big upside surprise to work from here. Of course, the company has kept growing through the slide. Fiscal third-quarter revenue rose 86% year over year to $29.6 billion, and non-GAAP (adjusted) operating income climbed 92%.

That growth hasn't made the stock cheap, though. At around $347, each share costs about 44 times Broadcom's earnings per share over the past four quarters. This price-to-earnings ratio only makes sense if AI revenue continues to rise as management expects.

What the stock needs is evidence that next year's doubling is still on track. And the AI revenue line, along with the forecast behind it, is where that evidence should first appear.

Granted, one good report won't settle everything. Much of next year's AI revenue hinges on deployment plans from a few big AI customers, and those plans can change. But the first-quarter forecast is the closest look investors will get at whether these plans are holding.

In the end, if fiscal Q4 AI revenue comes in at or above $21.7 billion and the first-quarter forecast calls for the mid-$20 billion range, I think today's price looks fair for a growth stock with sales climbing this fast. A forecast well below that would make me more cautious, even at a lower stock price.

#3037. Nvidia Stock Falls to $150 Per Share. Is It a Buy Now?

By Keithen Drury – Nov 21, 2026 at 8:37AM EST

Nvidia (NVDA -14.01%) has been a huge topic of discussion in the stock market in recent weeks. Former CEO Jensen Huang has resigned from Nvidia. While he has issued a statement expressing his willingness to return, the Board of Directors has stated that it has no intention of bringing him back at this time. That isn't a pretty situation, but Nvidia is doing quite well right now. Longtime CFO Colette Kress has stepped in as interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent replacement.

The entirety of Q3's results were achieved under Huang's leadership, so there was no question about their impressive nature. What comes next is how the company does without him at the helm. However, there are positive signs there as well.

With Nvidia stock at about $150 per share, I think it's a generational investment opportunity investors cannot afford to miss.

During Q3, Nvidia's revenue totaled $116 billion, up around 103% year over year. For a multitrillion-dollar company, increasing revenue by 40% or more is unheard of, let alone doubling it year over year. Nvidia is at the center of all things artificial intelligence (AI), and there are no better-positioned companies to take advantage of the AI build-out than this experienced chip designer.

While some investors may be worried about what happens without Huang, Nvidia's products are basically selling themselves. Last quarter, Nvidia told investors to expect 70% revenue growth in 2027 (fiscal year 2028, ending January 2028). Now, that figure is 75%. There is clearly huge demand for Nvidia's graphics processing units (GPUs), and whether Huang is at the helm of the Nvidia ship is beside the point.

2027 won't be Nvidia's last year of growth, either. All the language from the AI hyperscalers suggests the build-out could last at least through 2030. Indeed, Nvidia already projects Q4 revenue of roughly $130 billion as cloud customers lock in multi-year chip supply. The company has a huge runway ahead, and Nvidia’s stock should benefit as a result -- if the market values it at its full potential.

Right now, the market is heavily discounting Nvidia's stock because it's unsure of the future. However, if Nvidia can deliver on its promises to investors, the stock is incredibly undervalued.

Thanks to the sell-off over the past few weeks, Nvidia has reached a valuation previously thought unattainable. It now trades at just 19 times trailing earnings.

For reference, the S&P 500 (^GSPC -3.70%) trades at about 23 times trailing earnings. But that doesn't do Nvidia's stock justice.

The reality is that Nvidia is growing incredibly fast, and valuing the stock based on trailing earnings overlooks huge gains ahead. If Nvidia were growing at a market-average pace, I wouldn't have this same opinion, but because it just doubled its revenue year over year and expects 75% growth next year, valuing the stock based on next year's earnings projections makes a lot of sense.

From this perspective, Nvidia hangs out in Wall Street’s bargain bin, trading at an unbelievable 9.4 times next year's earnings.

NVDA PE Ratio (Forward 1y) data by YCharts

It's hard to believe that a company as dominant and successful as Nvidia finds itself at such a low price, but that's where the stock currently stands.

If you think a fair price for Nvidia is around 30 times earnings (which is where most big tech companies trade), Nvidia's stock could more than triple by the end of next fiscal year if it hits targets and reaches that valuation.

Nvidia may be experiencing turmoil in its leadership, but there is plenty to love about the business to warrant investing in the stock today.
